items.title: Looking and Gazing: Incidental Sight Versus Deliberate Attention

items.zh: 所言覩者，謂於如前所列諸事，若往、若還，先無覺慧、先無功用、先無欲樂，於其中間眼見眾色，是名為覩。所言瞻者，謂於如前所列諸事，若往、若還，覺慧為先、功用為先、欲樂為先，眼見眾色。謂或諸王，或諸王等，或諸僚佐，或諸黎庶，或婆羅門，或諸居士，或饒財寶長者商主，或餘外物、房舍、屋宇、殿堂、廊廟，或餘世間眾雜妙事，觀見此等，是名為瞻。
items.en: Incidental sight means: in the course of going or returning on the affairs already listed, without any prior deliberation, effort, or intention, one's eyes happen to fall on various forms along the way — this is called incidental sight. Deliberate gazing means: in the course of going or returning on those same affairs, with deliberation, effort, and intention leading the way, one's eyes take in various forms — kings, or those of equal rank, or ministers, or common people, or brahmins, or householders, or wealthy elders and merchants, or other external things such as dwellings, rooftops, halls, and galleries, or various other marvellous things of the world. Observing such things is called deliberate gazing.

items.zh: 若復於此覩瞻自相，能正了知；於所應覩，於所應瞻，能正了知；於應覩時，於應瞻時，能正了知；如所應覩，如所應瞻，能正了知；是名正知。彼由成就此正知故，自知而覩，自知而瞻；覩所應覩，瞻所應瞻；於應覩時，於應瞻時，而正瞻覩；如所應覩，如所應瞻，如是而覩，如是而瞻。如是名為若覩、若瞻正知而住。若屈、若申正知住者，云何為屈？云何為申？云何名為若屈、若申正知而住？

items.title: Bending and Stretching: Clear Awareness Down to Each Limb

items.zh: 謂彼如是覩時、瞻時，若往為先、若還為先，或屈申足、或屈申臂、或屈申手、或復屈申隨一支節，是名屈申。若於屈申所有自相，能正了知；若所屈申，能正了知；若屈申時，能正了知；若如是屈及如是申，能正了知；是名正知。
items.en: Whether while thus looking or gazing, or leading into going or returning, one bends or extends the foot, or bends or extends the arm, or bends or extends the hand, or bends or extends any other limb — this is called bending and stretching. Correctly knowing the mark of the bending or stretching itself; correctly knowing what part is bent or stretched; correctly knowing when it is bent or stretched; correctly knowing that it is bent or stretched exactly so — this is clear awareness.

items.zh: 彼由成就此正知故，於屈於申，自知而屈，自知而申；於所應屈，於所應申，而屈而申；於應屈時，於應申時，而屈而申；如所應屈，如所應申，如是而屈，如是而申。如是名為若屈、若申正知而住。持僧伽胝及以衣鉢正知住者，云何持僧伽胝？云何持衣？云何持鉢？云何持僧伽胝及以衣鉢正知而住？

items.title: Section: Carrying the Robes and Bowl With Clear Awareness

items.zh: 謂有大衣，或六十條、或九條等、或兩重刺，名僧伽胝。被服受用，能正將護，說名為持。若有中衣，若有下衣，或持為衣，或有長衣，或應作淨，或已作淨，如是一切說名為衣。被服受用，能正將護，說名為持。若堪受持或鐵、或瓦乞食應器，說名為鉢。現充受用，能正將護，說名為持。若於如是或僧伽胝、或衣、或鉢所有自相，能正了知；於所應持或僧伽胝、或衣、或鉢或淨不淨，能正了知；若於此時或僧伽胝、或衣、或鉢已持應持，能正了知；若於如是或僧伽胝、或衣、或鉢應如是持，能正了知；是名正知。
items.en: The great robe — whether of sixty strips, or nine strips, or made double-layered — is called the saṅghāṭī. Wearing and using it, properly protecting it, is called holding it. There is also the middle robe and the lower robe; there may be robes held [as one's own], or extra robes, robes yet to be formally consecrated, or robes already consecrated — all of these together are called robes. A begging-bowl of proper measure, capable of being maintained, whether of iron or clay, is called the bowl. Keeping it presently fit for use, properly protecting it, is called holding it. Correctly knowing the specific nature of the great robe, the robes, or the bowl; correctly knowing which one should be held, and whether it is consecrated or not; correctly knowing, at this time, which is already held and which should be held; correctly knowing that the great robe, the robes, or the bowl should be held exactly so — this is clear awareness.

items.zh: 彼由成就此正知故，於所應持或僧伽胝、或衣、或鉢，自知而持；於所應持，於應持時，而能正持；如所應持，如是而持。如是名為持僧伽胝及以衣鉢正知而住。若食、若飲、若噉、若甞正知住者，云何為食？云何為飲？云何為噉？云何為甞？云何若食、若飲、若噉、若甞正知而住？謂諸所有受用飲食，總名為食。此復二種，一、噉，二、甞。云何為噉？

blocks.text: Three more everyday contexts for clear awareness. Several short passages are untranslated.

"Without prior deliberation, the eyes happen to fall on various forms: this is incidental sight (覩)." "With deliberation leading the way, the eyes take in forms: this is looking (瞻)." Master Cháng Bǎi: for example, going to the hospital to see old age and sickness on purpose. Venerable Miào Jìng: "when you look, know that you are looking; don't look while entertaining other idle thoughts."
"One bends or extends the foot, the arm, the hand, or any other limb" with clear awareness. Master Cháng Bǎi: these movements are "expressive form" (表色), one of the kinds of form met on Day 3.

The great robe (saṅghāṭī), the upper robe, the lower robe; the bowl "of proper measure, iron or clay". Master Cháng Bǎi: too small and you can't eat enough; too big and it's a burden. Extra robes are made allowable through "pure giving" (作淨), a rule the Buddha set to free monks from attachment to possessions.

The detail can seem remote for a lay reader. But the principle is universal: every ordinary action, even picking up a cup, can be done with full awareness. The monastic rules are a training ground for that awareness.

quiz.q: What does the treatise call 覩, and which of the five minds does Venerable Miào Jìng match it to?
options: closing the eyes; the continuing mind
seeing forms along the way without prior deliberation, effort, or intention; the sudden mind
quiz.why: "Without any prior deliberation, effort, or intention, one's eyes happen to fall on various forms along the way — this is called incidental sight." Venerable Miào Jìng: not intentional — among the five minds, this is the sudden mind.

quiz.q: What example does Master Cháng Bǎi give for deliberate gazing?
options: going to the hospital when ill — intending to see a doctor
quiz.why: "With deliberation, effort, and intention leading the way, one's eyes take in various forms." Master Cháng Bǎi: for example, going to the hospital when ill is intending to see the doctor — that is 瞻.

quiz.q: What is the simplest requirement of clear awareness in looking, according to Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: when looking, know that you are looking, without thinking of other things
look at as much as possible
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: when you look, know that you are looking — don't look while entertaining other idle thoughts.

quiz.q: What does "bending and stretching" refer to, and what everyday example does Venerable Miào Jìng give?
options: bending or extending the foot, arm, hand, or any limb; knowing your arm extends and returns when picking up food with chopsticks
quiz.why: "One bends or extends the foot, or bends or extends the arm, or bends or extends the hand, or bends or extends any other limb." Venerable Miào Jìng: when you eat and reach with chopsticks for food, know that your arm has gone out and come back.

quiz.q: What is the saṅghāṭī, and how does Venerable Miào Jìng arrive at "sixty strips"?
options: the great robe of sixty or nine strips or doubled; a fifteen-strip robe has four pieces per strip, four times fifteen is sixty
quiz.why: "The great robe — whether of sixty strips, or nine strips, or sewn with double stitching — is called the saṅghāṭī." Venerable Miào Jìng: three long pieces plus one short make four; four times fifteen is sixty strips, sixty pieces.

quiz.q: The bowl is the "vessel of proper measure." How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "proper measure"?
options: too small and one can't eat enough to practise; too big and one can't finish — it must be just right
quiz.why: "A begging-bowl of proper measure, capable of being maintained, whether of iron or clay, is called the bowl." Master Cháng Bǎi: too small and you can't eat enough to practise; too big and you can't finish — just right is what makes a bowl.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "formally consecrating" (作淨) robes?
options: also called pure giving or declaring purity — a procedure the Buddha set to purify monks' attachment to possessions
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: 作淨 is also called pure giving or declaring purity — a rule the Buddha set to cleanse monks of attachment, hence "pure giving."
